newsitem.title: USA: Georgia nursing homes sue over Medicaid freeze.
newsitem.headline: Georgia nursing homes sue over Medicaid freeze.

text.p: Georgia Nursing Home Association said Thursday it has filed a lawsuit challenging the state's decision to freeze daily Medicaid payments for fiscal 1998.
The lawsuit was filed in U.S. District Court in Atlanta against the state, Georgia Department of Medical Assistance and department Commissioner Marjorie Smith.
It claims the freeze was unconstitutional and unlawful and jeopardizes the quality of care for 32,000 Medicaid recipients in Georgia nursing homes.
In April, Gov. Zell Miller vetoed the General Assembly's appropriation of $4.1 million to fund a Medicaid rate increase to cover inflation and minimum wage increases for fiscal 1998.
The association said that unless Miller reverses the veto, the state will lose an additional $8 million in federal matching funds.

"If the Governor insists on taking away our funding, the quality of care will suffer and, in the end, nursing home residents and their families will suffer the most," Association President Fred Watson said.
Miller's press spokesman, Rick Dent, said the governor would have no comment because "Our policy is not to comment on litigation."

Georgia's daily Medicaid reimbursement rate for nursing homes averages $75, which covers a resident's room, food, and 24-hour nursing care, among other services. The association said that rate is lower than that of 37 other states.
Medicaid helps four out of five Georgia nursing-home residents pay for their care.

The association said Georgia nursing homes have already absorbed $61 million in state Medicaid budget cuts in fiscal 1997. Based on the projected rate of inflation and at the current rate of Medicaid reimbursement, more than 80 percent of Georgia nursing homes will be forced to bear losses in 1998 for their Medicaid residents, Watson said.
Medicaid reimbursements will not be adequate to cover the costs of providing care and services for the elderly poor. Our system is already bare bones," he said.
